item.title: Seeds to Systems Cohort - Week 3: Community infrastructure, decision making & reviewing grant proposals
item.description:
Seeds to Systems is a cohort-based training and mentoring programme centred on organisational infrastructure for the sustainability of open research projects and communities. Each week, we share what the cohort sessions covered and some insights and questions they raised.

This week’s sessions

  • Session 5: Community infrastructure and decision making: We started by reflecting on what community infrastructure is, and how much of it becomes visible only when something breaks. Arielle Bennett then led a session on the explicit and implicit values and structures that shape how decisions are made in our projects, and on the gap between how decisions are supposed to be made and how they are actually made.
  • Session 6: Reviewing grant proposals: Daniela Saderi and Chad Sansing from PREreview introduced how systemic and personal bias can shape research review, and guided us through a live review of a past OLS grant proposal, with a focus on reflecting on what we bring as reviewers and offering feedback that is clear, constructive, and actionable.

Insights and emerging questions

When we asked what comes to mind when thinking about community infrastructure, answers went well beyond tools: roles and responsibilities, communication channels, governance, codes of conduct, onboarding new members, among others. As Susan Leigh Star noted, “the normally invisible quality of working infrastructure becomes visible when it breaks” (1999, p. 382). Many of the examples shared during the session showed what that can look like in practice: when something broke, it often revealed how much of the project’s work depended on specific people, or that responsibilities had never been clearly defined. Arielle Bennett then looked at what remains invisible from another angle. Drawing on Jo Freeman’s The Tyranny of Structurelessness, she reminded us that there is no such thing as a structureless group. When a community does not make its structures explicit, they still exist, but only those already on the inside can see and use them. Implicit structures can work well in some cases, and not every decision needs the whole community. What matters is that people know how decisions are made and how they can be questioned. It also matters whether those structures work as described: what is written down and what happens in practice can drift apart, sometimes without anyone noticing. In our second session this week, Daniela Saderi and Chad Sansing from PREreview guided us through grant review, starting from the idea that every reviewer brings personal and systemic biases to a proposal, shaped by wider systems that also run through research and its funding. Reflecting on what we bring before we start reading can help reduce their impact on our feedback. The next step, reading a proposal to understand it before judging it, was the hardest part for many of us. When it comes to writing feedback, a review can also help strengthen the proposed work, especially when it is clear and actionable, and recognises what already works well. The exercise also brought us back to our first week: without the funding call, it was hard to assess the proposal, because a proposal is always read in relation to what a call asks for. It can be well written and still not respond to it.

These conversations also left us with some open questions: Whose work keeps our community infrastructure running, and is that work visible to the rest of the community? If someone joined our community tomorrow, could they find out how decisions are made, and who makes them? What could reviewing other people’s proposals teach us about writing our own?

Resources

Session recordings and slides will be published on the Seeds to Systems resources page. To go deeper into this week’s topics, you can also explore these links shared during the sessions:

  • Community infrastructure:
    • The Ethnography of Infrastructure (Star, 1999)
    • MOCHA: How to Assign Responsibilities (The Management Center)
    • Right Kind of Wrong: The Science of Failing Well (Edmondson, 2023)
  • Decision making:
    • The Tyranny of Structurelessness (Freeman, 1970)
    • Governing the Commons (Ostrom, 1990)
  • Reviewing grant proposals:
    • Grant Bias Reflection Guide
    • Open Grant Reviewers Reviewer Guide

What’s next

Next week, we’ll hear from people working in research funding about how funding calls are designed and what happens behind the scenes of a funding decision. We’ll also look at how outreach and visibility support a project’s sustainability, including how to build a communications plan, and at how open science communities can measure the impact of their work.

item.title: Seeds to Systems Cohort - Week 2: Collaboration and equity
item.description:
Seeds to Systems is a cohort-based training and mentoring programme centred on organisational infrastructure for the sustainability of open research projects and communities. Each week, we share what the cohort sessions covered and some insights and questions they raised.

This week’s sessions

  • Session 3: Collaborations and community mapping: With Angela Okune, we explored how the word “collaboration” can hide very different expectations, and how naming them can help teams build agreements they can revisit as the work changes. Cassandra Gould van Praag then introduced community mapping as a way to understand who is part of a project, how people are connected, and where to focus engagement.
  • Session 4: Equity and collaborations panel: Batool Almarzouq invited us to rethink how equity is addressed in open science, looking beyond charity-based approaches to question how research funding is structured and who benefits from it. In a panel that followed, Alexander Martínez (LA-CoNGA Physics and EL-BONGÓ Physics) and Rowland Mosbergen (Equersa) shared their experiences of building collaborations and partnerships across different contexts.

Insights and emerging questions

Many of this week’s conversations were about things that usually go unsaid. In our session on collaboration, “collaboration” turned out to be one word holding very different expectations about time, credit, data, or who decides. When these remain unspoken, each person fills the word with their own meaning, and a collaboration can drift even when everyone involved has good intentions. Naming these assumptions, writing them down, and revisiting them as the work changes can help, but it also takes time: collaboration rarely saves time, and it needs room for building trust and reaching agreements. Community mapping raised a similar point from another angle. In many communities, only one or two people hold most of the knowledge about community members, their work, and who to connect with. Making that knowledge explicit makes it transferable, so it does not disappear when someone leaves, and helps distinguish connections that exist on paper from those where people actually work together.

Our second session this week turned to what is rarely said about research funding itself. Equity in open science is often discussed in broad terms, and inequity is framed as a lack of resources or skills, which leads to responses based on aid or capacity building. The session invited us to look instead at how funding is structured and who benefits from it: the money that funds open science is itself part of a wider economic system, and interventions that do not question that system, including openness itself, can end up reproducing the inequities they aim to address. Moving from charity-based to justice-based approaches means making these structures visible and asking who gets to produce knowledge, whose knowledge counts, and who decides. The panel brought some of these ideas into practice, from designing collaborations together and sharing responsibilities from the start, to documenting work so a project can outlive the people involved, to protecting volunteers’ time and making sure decisions are made by people from the regions where the work happens.

These conversations also left us with some open questions:

  • Do we know why each of our partners is collaborating with us, and do they know why we are?
  • Do the people in our community know what information we hold about them, who can access it, and how we use it?
  • Do our open science and inclusion practices challenge existing inequities, or work around them?
  • In our collaborations across regions, whose knowledge and priorities shape the work, and where does that power come from?

Resources

Session recordings and slides will be published on the Seeds to Systems resources page. To go deeper into this week’s topics, you can also explore these links shared during the sessions:

  • Collaboration:
    • Research Collaboration Agreement template (Okune, 2019)
    • Partos Power Awareness Tool
    • 4 Decision-Making Methods for Decentralised Teams (Bartlett, 2020)
    • Toward a comprehensive theory of collaboration (Wood and Gray, 1991)
    • A new form of collaboration in cultural anthropology: Matsutake Worlds (Choy et al., 2009)
    • Global Health Research in an Unequal World: Ethics Case Studies from Africa (Aellah, Chantler and Geissler, 2016)
  • Community mapping:
    • RCM-CRM, an open-source toolkit for mapping research communities
    • On data privacy and protection
    • Turing Environment and Sustainability Community Map
    • UK TRE map participant information sheet, an example of a consent model
    • Analyzing who is relevant to engage in environmental decision-making processes by interests, influence and impact: the 3i framework (Reed et al., 2025)
    • Reimagining the language of engagement in a post-stakeholder world (Reed et al., 2024)
  • Equity:
    • Rethinking Open Science Through Dependency Theory (Almarzouq, 2025)
    • Here’s Why Foreign Aid Is a Scam
    • Conversations on Dependency Theory
    • The Divide: A Brief Guide to Global Inequality and Its Solutions (Hickel, 2018)

What’s next

Next week, we’ll reflect on what community infrastructure is, and explore the explicit and implicit values and structures that shape how decisions are made in our projects. We’ll also practise reviewing grant proposals, with a focus on recognising and reducing the impact of bias on our feedback.

item.title: One Year of OLS's Fiscally Sponsored Communities Programme
item.description:
In November 2025 I joined OLS as the first dedicated staff member on the organisation’s Fiscally Sponsored Communities Programme. One year on: what have we been up to?

Our ongoing communities continue to go from strength to strength. RCM Co-op continues to establish themselves as a centre of excellence and expertise for research community management in the UK and beyond. We employ one member of staff through OLS, and hope to bring on a second one soon. RSE AUNZ have just finished organising three Research Software conferences, aiming to build and strengthen communities of research software engineers across Asia-Australia, Latin America, and Africa: and they’ve already started organising for 2027.

Our fiscal sponsorship programme isn’t just for long-term arrangements. We acted as UK fiscal host for this year’s Open Science Retreat, organised by the Digital Research Academy and held in Machynlleth, Wales. While we’ll be ending the fiscal sponsorship relationship soon, we still collaborate with DRA on other projects like OSPARK (and you might just see some OLS folks at next year’s retreat in Germany!).

This year, we started hosting Incubation Fellows: individuals who are building open research communities. These placements are designed to be fixed term, to enable Fellows to focus on building out stable and sustainable community infrastructure. Jyoti Bhogal is currently developing RSE Asia Association (including collaborating with RSE AUNZ on the RSE Asia-Australia conference). Ella Kaye from rainbowR has completed her fellowship, with rainbowR establishing itself as a financially independent organisation after a successful first conference held in February 2026. Ella told us what she learned in a blog post earlier this year.

Behind the scenes, a lot of work has gone in to building out processes and policies to help our fiscal sponsorship programme run smoothly: from an array of github issues to manage grant applications and contracts on behalf of our organisations, to reviewing internal policies and procedures to check that they cover our global community, to helping troubleshoot missing honoraria payments and last minute budget reviews. While I’m the only dedicated FSC member of staff, the programme couldn’t run without finance, comms and management colleagues from across the UK and the Americas. We work mostly remotely, but we did get to spend a few days together on a farm in the UK in June on OLS’s annual retreat (pictured above): making sure our programmes are learning from each other, planning for the future, and meeting some friendly cows, chickens and goats.

Heading into 2027, I’m excited to report that we’re in talks with some new communities who are interested in OLS fiscal hosting. If you’re working on open research and you think your community might benefit from fiscal sponsorship, you can read more about what it entails on our website: please do get in touch if you’d like to discuss this with us!

item.title: Seeds to Systems Cohort - Week 1: Welcome!
item.description:
Seeds to Systems is a cohort-based training and mentoring programme centred on organisational infrastructure for the sustainability of open research projects and communities. Each week, we share what the cohort sessions covered and some insights and questions they raised.

This week’s sessions

  • Session 1: Welcome: We kicked off the cohort by getting to know the teams and their projects, introducing how the programme will work, and opening a first conversation about what project and community sustainability means across very different contexts.
  • Session 2: Reading funding calls: We reflected on how reading funding calls is a skill often learned implicitly, and practised approaching a call as part of a wider network of documents, such as eligibility and evaluation criteria or guidance for applicants, to understand what funders expect beyond what they state explicitly.

Insights and emerging questions

When teams shared what sustainability means for their projects in our first session, funding came up often, but rarely on its own. Many described sustainability as building something that can continue beyond the people who started it, whether that means surviving leadership transitions, growing beyond a core team or a host institution, or keeping going after a particular funding stream ends. Others pointed out that sustainability is as much human as financial: much of the work that keeps open research communities going happens alongside people’s main jobs, often unpaid, and depends on keeping volunteers engaged without burning out the core team. Several teams also noted that funding tends to support the research itself, but not the community work behind it, such as governance or keeping volunteers engaged. Our second session echoed this from another angle. A funding call rarely matches a whole project: more often, it supports one part of it, and part of the work in reading a call is recognising where the project and the funder’s priorities already align. That kind of reading is itself a skill that most of us learn implicitly. Unlike research papers, for example, which some of us learn to write by first reading many of them, successful proposals are seldom available, formats change from funder to funder, and understanding what a call actually asks for often means connecting information across several documents. Feeling “in the dark” when starting to apply for funding is therefore a common experience, shaped by access to examples, mentors, networks, and time. Reading a call together also showed how much a single reader can miss, and how much we gain from making sense of these documents collectively. These conversations also left us with some open questions:

  • Sustainability often becomes a question when something changes: people leave, funding ends, or the community grows. How can we start thinking about it before that happens?
  • Reading a call and connecting all its related documents takes time: is that time accounted for when we plan an application? Who can afford it?
  • Having more applications openly available could help other projects and communities learn how to apply, including from those that were not funded. But is everyone in a position to share those?

Resources

Session recordings and slides will be published on the Seeds to Systems resources page. To go deeper into this week’s topics, you can also explore these links shared during the sessions:

  • Some examples of funding applications that are openly available:
    • From OLS
    • From the Open Infrastructure Fund

What’s next

Next week, we’ll turn to collaboration. We’ll explore the different relationships we call “collaboration” and how naming them can help teams build shared agreements, as well as how stakeholder mapping can support decision-making and strategy. We’ll also rethink how equity is addressed in open science funding, and hear from a panel of guests about building partnerships and trust across different contexts.

item.title: 📖 OLS Journal Club: Arnstein’s Ladder of Citizen Participation
item.description:
Power is important. It governs who gets to take decisions and about what, and who gets to benefit from the outcome of those decisions. In open research, we encounter issues related to power all the time: power dynamics can exist based on who has funding and who doesn’t; who has a stable position at a Global North institution and who is working precariously in a low-resource environment; who has lived experience of a particular condition or situation, and who has learned about it from books and papers. In fact, a lot of open research work seeks to rebalance power and to make all parts of research more accessible to those who might not otherwise have access.

To address power imbalances, however, we need to understand them. In my research work – first in human rights, and later in critical technology studies – there’s one framework I keep coming back to, as a way of being more thoughtful about what participatory research really looks like. It’s nearly 60 years old, but still resonates today.

Sherry Arnstein was a health and public policy specialist in the USA. Working at what is now the Department of Health and Human Services in the 1960s, she led the development of the strategy to desegregate all US hospitals, and worked on Lyndon B Johnson’s ‘War on Poverty.’ In 1969, she synthesised her experiences involving citizens and residents in decision-making into one framework: the Ladder of Citizen Participation1.

In her article, Arnstein draws on concrete examples from the US policy context to illustrate that ‘participation’ in decision-making can mean a wide swathe of activities: some of which rebalance power, and some of which merely cement existing hierarchies. At the bottom of her ladder is ‘participation’ that is in fact not participatory at all: where individuals are involved in decision-making processes only to rubber stamp decisions that have already been made, or are asked to participate in activities designed to change them, not unjust power dynamics.

Further up the ladder is tokenism: people are informed of decisions only after they have already taken place, or asked for their opinions through surveys and public hearings with no guarantee that these opinions will be taken into account when decisions are made. At most, participation may be placatory: a small number of people may sit on decision-making bodies (where they can be outvoted) or may be put on their own committees or working groups to ‘advise’ the groups that actually take the decisions: again with no guarantee of impact.

At the top of the ladder are what Arnstein termed ‘degrees of citizen power:’ working partnerships between decision-makers and citizens, and delegated power where public groups have successfully assumed responsibility for some decisions. At the top: citizen control, where the participants have full power over all decisions that are made.

Arnstein was drawing on her experience in city and community planning exercises, where she observed most of these ‘rungs’ on her ladder first-hand. But her ladder is much more widely applicable, which is why her article has been continuously reprinted and translated since its publication. Though Arnstein herself acknowledged that real participatory processes are more complicated than 8 simple positions, and that neither decision-makers nor the populations they serve are homogeneous groups, the ladder still serves as a useful guide for those of us who seek to make our work ‘more participatory.’ What ‘rung’ of the ladder are we actually aiming for, and what have we actually achieved? How much power are we willing to cede to our participants?

  1. Arnstein, S. R. (1969). A Ladder Of Citizen Participation. Journal of the American Institute of Planners, 35(4), 216–224. https://doi.org/10.1080/01944366908977225 ↩

item.title: OLS Spotlight 🔦 Sara Villa
item.description:
The spotlights of this month are all turned to Sara Villa, our Training and Community lead! She’s the happy face behind our warm Slack messages, training onboarding sessions, and our newsletter Roots.

Meet Sara!

Name: Sara Villa

Role in OLS: Training and Community Lead

Contact if people want to have a chat? sara [at] we-are-ols.org or drop me a Slack message!

Socials: LinkedIn

Questions about OLS

What do you do at OLS? What does your day look like?

My work days look very different and that’s what I love about working in OLS. One day I’m focusing on comms and spending time publishing blogs, posting on Slack and social media… Maybe next one I’m preparing training materials and researching new content… and other I’m in meetings all day talking to amazing people and LEARNING A LOT! As community and training lead, I do all this to make sure that OLS training efforts are the best quality and really serve our diversity and inclusion values. I love talking to different people and collaborating with them to improve every bit of work I get out.

What do you like about the OLS community? What makes it ‘different’?

OLS community is made of people who were humble enough to sign up to improve their own work, make it open and more accessible to others… and who love to collaborate with other people! That’s not something you can find in any community. We have global members with different expertise and backgrounds, who yet speak the same language: a love for research and sustainability to make the world better 🫶

How would you like to help people in the OLS community? What kind of help would you like from the OLS community?

I would love to help people get the word out about what an amazing work they’re already doing! If you want to write a blog post about your open work… help me to help you! I also enjoy making connections and putting people in touch so they can get the best of each other.

Questions about you and your interest

What skill/expertise do you have in the open science world? How did you learn it?

Efficient collaboration and facilitation. I think I learnt it by practice, one way or another, and they realised how relevant it is in the open science world. I love applying my skills to research and project management and to help others, so… win-win!

What is a topic that you care a lot about? Why is it important to you?

I care about continuous improvement, whether applying it to yourself, others, projects… anything in life! I think I love being a researcher because it’s the perfect way to improve things while helping yourself and others- so it pairs well with my incapacity to settle ;) I love applying continuous improvement not just as a tangible project management skill, but also as a reflective exercise to see how I can be a better person, a better colleague and a better human in this world.

Silly/short ones

What was your last impulsive buy?

Colouring mandala book

What is your guilty pleasure?

Vanilla ice cream- all day all year long

What is your favourite quote?

‘When you open your mind to the impossible, sometimes you find the truth’ (or really, anything by Walter Bishop in Fringe)

What item would you spend ALL YOUR money on?

Ice cream

What is your favourite movie?

My Neighbour Totoro

What is your favourite rainy day activity?

Watch my Neighbor Totoro while eating vanilla icecream XD

Deeper ones

What gets you out of bed?

My kid, hunger… and the hopes of a new day to have funnnnn!

What do you want to learn next in life?

How to keep doing research and science while nurturing communities.

What makes you sad?

Being 100% honest… hunger and being tired. Otherwise… I’m a pretty optimistic person!

What do you like about society?

The power of people and community. When it all goes to shit, people are always there and being human is what gets us out of any mess.

item.title: Fiscal Sponsorship: Ella Kaye & rainbowR
item.description:
Ella Kaye from rainbowR was an OLS Incubation Fellow from December 2025 to August 2026. We asked Ella to tell us about her work with rainbowR and how OLS helped her support the organisation:

Tell us about rainbowR!

rainbowR is a community which connects, supports and promotes LGBTQ+ folks who code in R and spreads awareness of LGBTQ+ issues through data-driven activism.

Tell us about yourself: how long have you been involved with rainbowR? What is your role?

Professionally, I’m a Senior Research Software Engineer at The University of Birmingham, where I work primarily to enable the next generation of contributors to R. I love R and the R community! I co-founded rainbowR back in 2017. The community went dormant a couple of years later. I revived it in 2022 and have been running it since then. Formally, I’m the chair of the leadership committee. There are lots of wonderful people involved in running rainbowR across the leadership, conference and CoC committees, and I’m keen for someone else to take on the role of chair soon.

What did rainbowR achieve during your Incubation Fellowship with OLS?

My OLS incubation fellowship overlapped with my SSI fellowship. My main aims were to nurture rainbowR and make it sustainable for the long term. Part of that was formalising the community governance structures and processes, and the other was delivering a rainbowR conference. During the OLS fellowship, rainbowR held an inaugural AGM and voted to adopt a proposed constitution and elect a leadership committee. We also held a two-day conference, which was a massive undertaking and a huge success!

How did fiscal sponsorship help you achieve those aims?

The fiscal sponsorship enabled rainbowR to raise money from the conference via donations and solidarity payments - OLS handled all the financial side for us. As rainbowR grows, so do our costs - the money we raised will cover us for at least the next couple of years. At the time, we were going through the process of formalising our governance so we could apply for our own bank account, but it wasn’t possible to align the timing to have that in place for the conference.

What would you have done differently during your fellowship?

I went along to a couple of the Friday co-working sessions. I really enjoyed chatting with other OLS folks at those, and they had lots of good suggestions and helpful recommendations for the conference. I wish I had attended more of them!

What is rainbowR up to now? Where can readers find out more about your next steps?

After the success of the conference earlier this year, we have just announced that we will run the conference again in 2027. We continue to run our monthly meet-ups and quarterly buddies scheme. The community as a whole continues to grow - we’ve welcomed ten new members in the last month. Find out more about us at https://rainbowr.org. If you’re LGBTQ+ and code in R and like the sound of hanging out with other such folks, join us!

item.title: OLS Spotlight 🔦 Yo Yehudi
item.description:
Have a look and discover a bit more about our wonderful Yo, co-executive director of OLS!

Meet Yo Yehudi

Name: Yochannah Yehudi / Yo Yehudi
Role in OLS: Chaos generator / Co-executive director
Contact if people want to have a chat? Yo at we are ols dot org :)
Socials: nah

Questions about OLS

What do you do at OLS? What does your day look like?

Breakfast and coffee at a leisurely pace with my book, please! A meeting at 10 AM is too early, honestly. I like having a slower start to my day. As co-executive director, my day tends to change a lot from week to week. Some constants are 1:1s with my direct reports (that’s Laura Carter, Riva Quiroga, and Irene Ramos), catchups with my co-exec Patricia Herterich, and weekly team catchups. I use reclaim.ai to help schedule breaks between meetings and enforce my calendar having lunchtimes in it, as well as using it to mirror between my personal calendar and work calendar. The other more varied things involve spending time networking with community, funders, clients, and others in the open research ecosystem, and reading, writing, reflecting. We build a lot of reflection time into our work as a team, with (roughly) quarterly 1:1 retrospectives, as well as project-specific retros. This helps us to learn from things that didn’t go well, so we can iterate and try new things - but also allows us to identify things that do go well, so we can be proud of ourselves and continue doing those bits. This gives us the space to take “failures” and make them “learnings” instead - a much more pleasant way to go through life.

What are your interests besides your OLS work?

Oh no, are you accusing me of having a life outside my job?! Just kidding ;) I love nature, and physical activities. My teenage self would find that hilarious as I did everything I could to get out of school physical activity lessons (known as “sport” lessons in Israel). The best way to make me “recharge” is to put me somewhere where there are more plants than humans for a few hours. In the past I’ve cycled long distance (UK Coast-to-Coast, other general bikepacking), run half-marathons, and done long distance hikes, most recently a week walking around the island of Jersey.

Silly/short ones

What is your go-to karaoke song?

Lol no

Cats or dogs?

Yes please!

What was your last impulsive buy?

Um, a plush Finch.

What would you like people to stop asking you about?

My pronouns. I don’t associate strongly with any gender and I hate how much people expect me to have a ‘standard’ gender identity. I wish the languages I spoke didn’t have gendered pronouns at all.

What mythical creature would you believe as real?

A Companion. Every time I see a white horse I will it to Choose me, but they usually just ignore me. I guess my mindspeech isn’t strong enough.

What is the strangest thing that you have seen while walking down the street?

In Glastonbury in 2014, I was corralled into participating in a show of some sort. We only communicated via mime, and I had to wear a silver swimsuit over my clothes, and sing certain notes on-cue.

What is your guilty pleasure?

Eating a whole tub of Ben & Jerry’s Cookies on Cookie Dough icecream in one go. I exercise a lot for my mental and physical wellbeing, and the ability to eat a lot is a nice side-effect.

What is your lazy go-to dinner?

Garlic pasta with lots of olive oil and not much else.

What ALWAYS makes you laugh?

A good pun or a poo joke.

DEEPER ONES

What is the meaning of life?

What we make of it, I reckon :) - for me that’s having a reasonably good time myself and trying to share the good times with others around me.

What gets you out of bed?

I know this is supposed to be a “deep” question but I really want to answer “either my bladder or a cat asking for breakfast”. I really enjoy lying in bed when it’s warm and snuggly, and maybe conning my spouse into getting me a coffee while I’m still in bed.

What do you wish you learned sooner?

I was forty years old when I learned that I was Autistic and had ADHD. It literally wasn’t possible to have been diagnosed with both when I was a child, as those two diagnoses used to be mutually exclusive. But damn, knowing I had a medically treatable condition (ADHD) and that I wasn’t just “naughty” or “a dreamer”…. That feels like I would have made one hell of a difference to my self esteem.

What do you like about society?

We, as humans, make speculative fiction. The thing about these books - often scifi or fantasy - is that they look at the world, say “what if this thing was different?” Then they take that difference and explore what society might be like. If volcanic eruptions were common, how might humanity survive? Can capitalism continue to thrive if there are light-years of distance between the enclaves of sentient beings? What might a whole world united under a single government look like, if it implemented universal basic income?

item.title: 📖 Book Report: Suspicious Minds by Rob Brotherton
item.description:
When I tell people that my PhD was about why people believe conspiracy theories, I often get quite an excited reaction. Most people immediately start asking me more about the topic! It’s something which many people are interested in, be it due to a relative who went down the rabbit hole or a personal fascination with UFOs. In some cases, I’m asked where to learn more about the psychology of conspiracy theories. My go-to recommendation is Suspicious Minds: Why We Believe Conspiracy Theories by Rob Brotherton.

The introductory chapters provide a fairly comprehensive overview of conspiracy theory research. It starts with what they actually are - something surprisingly contentious, especially since the academic definition of “conspiracy theory” doesn’t always match the way we use the phrase in everyday life. It also draws on historical, political, and sociological evidence to show that contrary to popular belief, they are not a modern phenomenon. Conspiracy theories have been recorded throughout history, such as during the Roman Empire and the Great Fire of London, and continue to be relatively widespread today.

There is also a clear explanation of why conspiracy theories can be harmful, with the MMR vaccine being one high-profile case study. However, the book does an excellent job of highlighting that the psychological processes driving belief in conspiracy theories are both normal and helpful. For example, the book explains how cognitive biases (such as incorrectly attributing causality) and social psychological processes (such as our tendency to attribute intentionality where it does not exist) contribute to conspiracy theory beliefs. These are important processes for navigating the world, as they let us identify patterns and understand the people around us. However, they also let us identify actual corruption and conspiracies where they occur.

At this point you might be wondering, “the psychology of conspiracy theories sounds cool, but why should I care?”. The simple answer is that open research has brought new ways that findings can be misused or misinterpreted. It could be incorrect use of the findings of open access publications; less-than-ideal analyses on open data sets; or backlash against fundamental open research values such as equity. If we understand why people believe conspiracy theories, then we can start to think of ways of addressing their relationship with open research practices. Open research and related concepts provide a lot of potential to increase trust in research, which may also reduce conspiracy theorising about our work as researchers. I think we should make the most of that!

So, is the book worth reading? I may be biased, but it’s a resounding yes from me! I think it provides a balanced summary of the cognitive and social psychology of conspiracy theory beliefs. It’s worth noting that the literature it cites is slightly outdated - it was published 10 years ago, after all - but that does not detract from its quality.

item.title: OLS Spotlight 🔦 Patricia Herterich
item.description:
Have a look and discover a bit more about our wonderful Patricia, co-executive director of OLS!

Meet Patricia Herterich

Name: Patricia Herterich
Role in OLS: OLS co-executive director
Contact if people want to have a chat? patricia [at] we-are-ols [dot] org - but please be patient, I’m not the fastest at answering emails.
Socials: LinkedIn

Questions about OLS

What do you do at OLS? What does your day look like?

Since September 2025, I’m co-executive director at OLS with a focus on OLS’s finances. My spouse would say that means I’m back to being a professional meeting-haver as the constants in my schedule are meetings with my direct reports (Bethan and Sara), check-ins with Yo Yehudi on OLS leadership things and meetings with the whole OLS core team and the community in co-working sessions. In addition, there are regular catch-ups with our accountants and key collaborators. The rest of my time is usually spent on finance spreadsheets and reporting, making sure our payments are correctly allocated and we have a good overview of the financial sustainability of the organization.

What are your interests besides your OLS work?

Before getting stuck into OLS leadership, some of my work focused on inclusive meetings. I organised big events (Collaborations Workshop 24), support events by value-aligned communities if I have capacity (The Turing Way book dash) and my experiences and research contributed to a paper written by OLS community members.

Questions about you and your interest

What skill/expertise do you have in the open science world? How did you learn it?

My main background is in research data management, especially in publishing research data in data repositories. I learned by doing: my first job after university (degree in library and information science) was at CERN building research data workflows and platforms. It required researching best practices of data repositories in other disciplines, deep dives into standards and many conversations with researchers to figure out how to make things easily usable for them.

What recent book/article/podcast have you come across that’s changed the way you see things?

Not an individual podcast episode, but I do like “The Wellness Scoop”. On reflection, I spent all my 20s trying to be an overachieving millennial thinking I need to track and perfect all parts of life. I do like the podcast as a reminder that at least concerning my body, I can ignore a lot of hypes and I’m actually doing ok.

Silly/short ones

What is your go-to karaoke song?

I haven’t done karaoke in a while (and if so, you book a box with friends - I’m not singing in front of a crowd of strangers) but I like singing and try to use Yousician for at least a few minutes a week. Songs I’m pretty good at are most things by John Denver. Songs I’ve liked in karaoke and miss on that app? “The Captain” by Biffy Clyro and some more German stuff that I’d be rather bad at but no one will know ;-).

Cats or dogs?

Yes :)

What is your favourite quote?

“I’m 100% tall.” (from Jonathan Safran Foer’s “Everything is illuminated”). Not inspirational but always true.

Deeper ones

What gets you out of bed?

Usually my bladder and if that doesn’t work, on most days guilt after having hit snooze a few times. I still run on external deadlines and demands, so I get up to unblock others and deliver the things I have promised them. I know this isn’t the healthiest motivation and something intrinsic to make the world a better place but be more inspirational.
